summary: Explains how OSPF routes can be computed over MPLS traffic-engineering tunnels set up using information from another OSPF instance, so one tunnel infrastructure can serve both IPv4 and IPv6 destinations. It does this by advertising cross-address-family information.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of building one bridge for each kind of car, this lets both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic share one bridge.

questions: ipv4 and ipv6 te tunnel sharing
what is cross address family ospf
how does ospf map te tunnels to routers
subtitle: Lets OSPF find the right tail-end router for traffic engineering tunnels built from the other address family's OSPF data.

tldr.problem: In a dual-stack network, MPLS TE tunnels may be duplicated for IPv4 and IPv6. A router running one OSPF instance cannot reliably map a tunnel's destination in the other address family to the right tail-end router.
tldr.mechanism: Each router advertises its local addresses of the other address family in the Node IPv4 or Node IPv6 Local Address sub-TLV. Head-end routers match tunnel destinations against these addresses to find the tail-end router and area.
tldr.outcome: One set of TE tunnels can serve both IPv4 and IPv6 routing. The RFC updates RFC 5786 and only tunnel endpoints need upgrading.

facts.label: X-AF address per ABR
facts.value: Advertised into at most one area

today: RFC 8687 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2019. It updates RFC 5786 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: One Tunnel Set for Two Address Families
sections.content:
Traffic engineering (TE) extensions exist for OSPFv2 (RFC 3630) and OSPFv3 (RFC 5329), but the TE database is tightly coupled to its own address family: IPv4 for OSPFv2 and IPv6 for OSPFv3. In a dual-stack network it can be better to use common MPLS TE label switched paths (LSPs) for both kinds of traffic. This halves the number of LSPs, eases scalability and management concerns, and lets operators group traffic by business needs, class of service or application.

To compute shortcut routes over TE tunnels, for example with the algorithm in RFC 3906, the head-end router must reliably map a destination address of the other address family to the corresponding tail-end router. That is hard because the routing LSAs live in one OSPF instance while the TE database may belong to another.

This document updates RFC 5786, which defined the Node IPv4 Local Address and Node IPv6 Local Address sub-TLVs of the Node Attribute TLV but did not describe their use when the advertised address family differs from the family of the OSPF TE protocol. The RFC lets a router announce one or more local cross-address-family (X-AF) addresses with these sub-TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of building one road for IPv4 cars and a second for IPv6 cars, build one road and teach everyone how to find the right house on it.

sections.title: Why Router IDs Are Not Enough
sections.content:
A simple idea is to identify a node by its Router ID in both the OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 link state databases. That would force both instances on a router to use the same Router ID, so correctness would depend on configuration, adding burden and cost. It gets worse if the two topologies differ, for example if area borders are chosen differently.

If the processes fall out of sync, there is no defined way for other routers to notice the mismatch and react, such as by avoiding the affected tunnels or alerting administrators. Misaligned Router IDs may deliver traffic to the wrong tail-end router, which could cause suboptimal routing or even traffic loops. Advertising addresses explicitly avoids relying on matching IDs.
sections.plainLanguage: Matching people by one shared ID badge only works if every office hands out the same badge. Listing each person's actual addresses is safer.

sections.title: What Routers Advertise
sections.content:
To use X-AF routing, OSPFv2 advertises the Node IPv6 Local Address sub-TLV and OSPFv3 advertises the Node IPv4 Local Address sub-TLV, possibly alongside other addresses allowed by RFC 5786. When OSPFv3 carries IPv4, multiple OSPFv3 instances are needed (RFC 5838); the text is written with OSPFv2 as the IPv4 protocol, the most common case.

On a node that implements X-AF routing, each OSPF instance advertises the X-AF local addresses usable by the Constrained Shortest Path First (CSPF) calculation for MPLS TE LSPs:

  • It MUST advertise the address listed in the Router Address TLV of the X-AF instance that maintains the TE database.
  • It SHOULD include additional local addresses advertised by the X-AF OSPF instance in its Node Local Address sub-TLVs.
  • It MAY advertise other local X-AF addresses.

If TE information is advertised in an instance both natively and as an X-AF Node Attribute TLV, local configuration decides which TE database is used to compute routes for that instance.

On Area Border Routers, each advertised X-AF address MUST be advertised into at most one area. If the OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 ABRs coincide, with the same areas for all interfaces, the X-AF addresses MUST go into the same area in both instances, so other ABRs know which area to associate with computed tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router writes its other-kind address in its card in the other phone book. The rules say which addresses it must, should or may list.

sections.title: Mapping Tunnels to Tail-End Routers
sections.content:
During the X-AF routing calculation, the router walks the list of MPLS TE tunnels for which it is the head end. For each tunnel T:

  1. If T's destination address is from the same address family as the OSPF instance of the LSDB, the extensions in this RFC do not apply.
  2. Otherwise it is an X-AF tunnel, so note its destination IP address.
  3. Walk the X-AF IP addresses in the LSDBs of all connected areas. If a match is found, advertised by router R in area A, mark T as belonging to area A and ending on tail-end router R, and assign the intra-area SPF cost to reach R in A as the IGP cost of T.

Afterwards each tunnel has an area, a tail-end router and a cost in terms of the routing LSDB. The algorithm is used only if the Node Local Address sub-TLV includes X-AF information. It is described as a single calculation for clarity, and implementations may use any equivalent mapping.

In the RFC's example, a router accepts TE LSPs ending at the local IPv4 addresses 198.51.100.1 and 198.51.100.2. OSPFv2 advertises 198.51.100.1 in the Router Address TLV and 198.51.100.2 in the Node IPv4 Local Address sub-TLV. An X-AF-enabled OSPFv3 instance advertises both addresses in the Node IPv4 Local Address sub-TLV, so other routers identify this router as the egress for LSPs ending at either address.
sections.plainLanguage: For each tunnel, look up its destination address in the other phone book. The match tells you which router is at the end and how far away it is.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Only routers that are endpoints of TE tunnels MUST be upgraded. Tail-end routers advertise the Node IPv4 and/or Node IPv6 Local Address sub-TLV, and head-end routers perform the X-AF calculation. Both endpoints MUST be upgraded before the tail end starts advertising X-AF information. Other routers do not need to support the X-AF procedures.

There is one interaction with optical networks. RFC 6827 also updates RFC 5786, for Automatically Switched Optical Networks (ASON), and requires the Local TE Router ID sub-TLV. If that sub-TLV is present in the Node Attribute TLV, the RFC 6827 procedures apply whether or not any X-AF information is advertised.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the two ends of each road need the new map. Everyone in between can carry on as before.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The Local Address sub-TLVs may already be advertised in any OSPF instance under RFC 5786, so no new threats arise beyond those in OSPFv2, OSPFv3 and RFC 5786. X-AF information is not used for SPF computation or normal routing, so it has no effect on IP routing itself.

Incorrect or tampered sub-TLVs can still affect TE computations. TE traffic may reach the wrong tail-end router, leading to suboptimal routing, traffic loops, or exposure of the traffic to inspection or modification by an attacker. These threats already exist in other TE specifications such as RFC 3630 and RFC 5329, whose considerations apply here. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone writes a wrong address in the phone book, traffic could end up at the wrong house. That risk already existed for the older books.

items.title: MUST
items.text: The Router Address TLV address of the X-AF instance holding the TE database.

items.title: SHOULD
items.text: Additional local addresses advertised by the X-AF instance.
